Hi all,

I used the search tool to check whether new contributions may be submitted under the GPL or LGPL, version 3, but I could not find a clear answer to this specific question.

I understand that Apache- and MIT-licensed code can, subject to the relevant licence conditions, be incorporated into GPL-licensed projects. What I am unsure about is whether code licensed under the GPL or LGPL can be contributed to a project that uses a different licence.

Could someone clarify which licences are acceptable for new contributions and, if GPLv3 or LGPLv3 are not acceptable, explain the reasons for excluding them? The GPL is the licence I am most familiar with, so I would appreciate understanding the rationale behind the project's licensing policy.

Uwe Brauer

IANAL but probably Apache 2 only.
Most of these licenses are sticky, so if you're contributing e.g. MIT-licensed code to Mathlib you'll have to also add the MIT license next to them. I think there's no precedent for this.

IMO formalizing maths is hard work enough that we shouldn't also subject Mathlib users to license conundrums, so a uniform license for all files makes sense. I also don't know of many software projects that have different licenses for different parts of the project.

No, definitely not. That would mean the project could no longer be used under the terms of the Apache license. You're welcome to write your own independent project under whatever license you prefer, but you can't put code with a more restrictive license into a project with a less restrictive license.

Unless you launder it through an LLM first, of course

The apache license even states explicitly that any code intended to be included in the licensed project (e.g. mathlib) must be under the same license with no additional terms, see point 5 of the license:

  1. Submission of Contributions. Unless You explicitly state otherwise,
    any Contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the Work
    by You to the Licensor shall be under the terms and conditions of
    this License, without any additional terms or conditions.
    Notwithstanding the above, nothing herein shall supersede or modify
    the terms of any separate license agreement you may have executed
    with Licensor regarding such Contributions.

Thank you, but I am now confused. Does the Apache Licence really prohibit contributions made available under a different licence, such as the (L)GPL? I had understood that this sort of restriction was characteristic of the GPL: new code can only be accepted if it is licensed under the GPL.

I had also understood the Apache Licence to be more permissive than the GPL. As I understand it, for example, someone can modify Mathlib and distribute the modified version under a restrictive commercial licence, subject to the conditions of the Apache Licence.

The only explanation I can think of for choosing such a permissive licence is that some Mathlib/Lean contributors may be prohibited by their employers from using GPL-licensed code.

I would be grateful for clarification.

I have looked into this further, and my understanding is that the distinction between Apache 2.0 and GPLv3 is essentially as follows.

  1. Suppose software is released under Apache 2.0 and I modify it. I can distribute and sell my modified version commercially, including under a proprietary licence and without publishing my source code. I must, however, comply with Apache 2.0's conditions, including retaining the relevant copyright and licence notices, supplying a copy of the licence and marking modified files appropriately. I cannot simply remove the original authors' copyright notices.

  2. Under GPLv3, I can also sell modified software commercially. The difference is that, when I distribute it, I must comply with the GPL's copyleft requirements: recipients must be able to obtain the corresponding source code, and the covered work must remain under the GPL's terms. I cannot distribute the modified version as proprietary software.

This is the distinction I have in mind: Apache 2.0 permits proprietary derivatives, whereas GPLv3 requires distributed derivatives of covered code to remain under the GPL.

The distinction is somewhat relevant to what OpenAI did on 6 October, when it released 377 mathematical results, without following estabilished traditions

My suspicion is that Apache 2.0 was chosen for Lean because its author was working at Microsoft and may have faced restrictions on using GPL-licensed code. Mathlib has the same licence, perhaps because it followed Lean's choice, but I wonder whether it could switch to the GPL.

I wonder whether it could switch to the GPL

Assuming for the sake of the argument that mathlib wants this: this seems very hard to pull of in practice, given the fact that mathlib has had in the order of 900 contributors over a span of nine to ten years.

I wonder whether it could switch to the GPL

Assuming for the sake of the argument that mathlib wants this: this seems very hard to pull of in practice, given the fact that mathlib has had in the order of 900 contributors over a span of nine to ten years.

That is now purely academic:

Do you mean that all 900 contributors would have to agree? My understanding is that this would not necessarily be required, provided the change applied only to new contributions.

New code and fixes could be licensed under the GPL, while the existing code remained under Apache 2.0. The key distinction is that Apache-licensed code can generally be incorporated into a GPLv3-licensed project, subject to the relevant licence conditions, but GPLv3-licensed code cannot simply be relicensed under Apache 2.0.

In that sense, the licensing change would be a one-way street: Apache-licensed code could be incorporated into a GPLv3-licensed version of Mathlib, but GPLv3-licensed contributions could not then be distributed under Apache 2.0 without the necessary permissions.

In practise a GPLv3 means most industrial applications cannot use the library. In industry it's very common to have license checkers deployed which explicitely check that nothing like GPL is integrated into your project, as open-sourcing might not be an option. I think for a "general purpose" library like mathlib, GPL3 might be quite harmful and apache2 is a reasonable choice.

For Lean4 as a language, GPL seems unthinkable: the language is actively also targetting industry applications like software- (or even hardware-) verification. Having lean4 licensed under GPL would likely prevent it from being used in any industrial application.

I dont think your suspicion about the decision process is accurate. I would assume the choice of license is certainly deliberate, taking into account the target audience and the envisioned future for lean and the lean universe

(sidenote: I certainly like GPL3 and have used it in some projects, my point here is merely that it isn't always a reasonable choice)

sorry, that was badly explained.
What I had in mind was an analogy. The GPLv3 is a form of “this for that”: I give you code, and you have to pay me back in code. (Payback.)
The same principle applies in mathematics. I prove a theorem and take care to present it in a way that others can use.
You use my theorem, generalise it, acknowledge my contribution and present your result in a form that others can use.
That is payback.
OpenAI has not done this. Above all, the proofs of the theorems (even those accompanied by Lean certificates) are incomprehensible and probably cannot be used by others. There is no (or little) payback.
